title: Elapsed Ticks Since a Free-Running Counter (MISRA Unsigned Arithmetic)
statement:
A free-running hardware tick counter -- a timer peripheral counting
milliseconds, say -- increments once per tick for as long as the board is
powered, and wraps back to `0` the instant it would overflow past
`UINT32_MAX`, rather than stopping. Working out how much time has passed
between two readings of that counter means handling the wrap correctly, not
just subtracting.

This one is written to **MISRA C:2012**, like *Linear Interpolation Over a Calibration Table*. The point of the
exercise is the *type*, not a longer algorithm.

## Your function

```
uint32_t ticks_elapsed(uint32_t now, uint32_t start);
```

Both `now` and `start` are readings of the same free-running counter. The
true elapsed time between them is guaranteed to be less than
`UINT32_MAX + 1` ticks -- true of any interval you would ever measure
against a 32-bit millisecond counter, which only wraps once every 49-odd
days. Return how many ticks elapsed between `start` and `now`, whether or
not the counter wrapped around in between.

## Why the whole answer is one line

`return now - start;` is not a shortcut -- it is the complete, correct
answer. Unsigned subtraction in C wraps modulo `2**32`, and that wraparound
is **well-defined behaviour**, not undefined behaviour the way signed
overflow is. Because the counter itself wraps the same way, `now - start`
computed modulo `2**32` recovers the true forward distance travelled
regardless of whether `now` is numerically less than `start`. This is
exactly the case Directive 4.6 exists for: `uint32_t` is not an arbitrary
choice of type here, it is the type whose defined-overflow arithmetic makes
the one-line answer correct in the first place.

## Watch out

- **Do not "fix" `now < start` with a branch.** Code like
  `if (now >= start) { result = now - start; } else { result = (UINT32_MAX - start) + now + 1; }`
  looks defensive but is just a hand-rolled, fencepost-prone reimplementation
  of what unsigned subtraction already does for free. Every fixed test that
  crosses the wrap boundary exists to catch that off-by-one.
- **Do not cast either operand to a signed type to "check the sign" of the
  difference.** `(int32_t)now - (int32_t)start` reintroduces the exact
  failure mode `uint32_t` was chosen to avoid: the true difference can
  itself exceed `INT32_MAX`, and signed overflow on top of that is
  undefined behaviour, not a negative number you can rely on.
